conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I understand you were admitted because you can’t tolerate eating or drinking much. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this burning pain in the middle of my upper belly, and it goes up into my chest like my esophagus. I’m nauseated all the time. I can only do water and shakes—no solid food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How long has this been happening, and have you been vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two days. I didn’t vomit until I got here—then I threw up once and it looked kind of red-tinged brown. Not like a lot of blood, but it scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you came in. Any black stools, fevers, chills, or trouble passing gas or having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. I’m still having bowel movements and passing gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, the reversal, and prior gastrojejunal ulcer—your symptoms could fit irritation or ulcer-type pain, but we also want to make sure there’s no narrowing, blockage, or leak. We’ll start with labs and an upper GI contrast study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this going to mean surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Right now our first step is to evaluate and support you—fluids, nausea control, and using your G-tube for nutrition if you can tolerate it. We’ll decide next steps based on the imaging and how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugars have been weird overnight. I even restarted my tube feeds at home and it didn’t fix it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Because of your post-gastric surgery hypoglycemia history, we’ll monitor your fingerstick blood sugars closely. While you’re not taking much in, we’ll use dextrose-containing IV fluids to keep things stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried about the burning in my chest—could it be my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pattern you describe sounds more like reflux or irritation along the esophagus, especially with the nausea and upper abdominal pain. We’ll keep an eye on your vital signs and symptoms, and if anything suggests a heart issue we’d evaluate that right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight, we’ll keep you on clear liquids as tolerated, give IV fluids, and use anti-nausea medication. Are you currently taking pantoprazole and sucralfate at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take both. I can’t take NSAIDs or aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect—avoiding NSAIDs is important for ulcers. We’ll continue your acid suppression and protectant medications here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated, and the burning pain is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do the upper GI study this morning. It’s a contrast X-ray where you swallow contrast and we watch it pass through. It helps us look for a leak, stricture, or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And what if I throw up during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t be painful, but the contrast can be unpleasant. If you feel nauseated, tell the radiology team—they can pause. We’ll also give anti-nausea medication beforehand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your upper GI study is back: no evidence of leak, stricture, or obstruction. There was mild reflux noted, which fits with the burning sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? Because I feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s no dangerous blockage or leak seen on that test, which is reassuring. But you can still have significant symptoms from ulcer irritation, reflux, or slow stomach emptying after your surgeries. Our goal now is to get your nutrition and nausea under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean tube feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll re-trial tube feeds through your G-tube, starting at a low rate and increasing slowly. We’ll keep the dextrose IV fluids while we ramp up so your blood sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started Vivonex through the G-tube at a low rate. How are you feeling with it running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At 30 it’s okay, but when they tried to go higher I got really nauseated and crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful feedback. If you can’t tolerate higher rates, we can switch to a more concentrated formula so you get the calories at a lower volume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to be sick all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll adjust stepwise—formula, rate, and nausea meds—so it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning we’re going to change the feeding plan. We’ll trial a more concentrated formula and see if your stomach tolerates it better at a lower rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the nausea medicine going to change too? Zofran helps a little but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since ondansetron hasn’t been enough, we’ll add prochlorperazine as needed. We’ll still use what works for you, but we want better control so you can tolerate feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented the feeding through the G-tube today and we’ll keep increasing carefully. Let us know right away if you feel worsening nausea, bloating, or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also anxious—every time I feel that burning I think something is tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense given your surgical history. The upper GI didn’t show a leak or obstruction, and your exam is reassuring. We’ll keep monitoring, and we’ll treat the reflux and nausea aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight with the new formula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than before. Still some nausea, but it’s not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re aiming for a goal rate that meets your nutrition needs. If you keep tolerating, we can work toward discharge with a home tube-feeding plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on tube feeds 24 hours a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least initially, yes—continuous feeds are often easier to tolerate. Your discharge plan may also include scheduled boluses depending on what you tolerate and what’s safest for your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar—are you seeing lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far your blood sugars have been stable with the dextrose IV fluids and the gradual feed increase. We’ll keep checking regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re switching you to Jevity 1.5 at a rate that should give you more nutrition with less volume. We’ll start and then work up toward 45 mL per hour if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s different about Jevity? Is it going to upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s more calorie-dense, so you don’t need as much volume per hour. Many people tolerate it better when volume is the limiting factor. We’ll go slowly and treat nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The prochlorperazine helped more than the Zofran. I’m sleepy though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sleepiness can happen with prochlorperazine. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and keep it as needed. Safety-wise, call the nurse before getting up if you feel drowsy or lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re up to a higher rate on Jevity now. Any vomiting or worsening abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The nausea comes and goes, but it’s manageable. The burning is less constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. If you continue to tolerate, we can start tapering the IV dextrose once your tube feeds are reliably at goal and your sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home and messing up the tube feeds. What if I can’t keep up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have a clear plan: the formula, the rate, and how to give the bolus flushes. Nursing will review the pump and G-tube care with you, and we’ll arrange supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re adding a medication called erythromycin. In low doses it can help stomach motility—basically help things move along—so feeds are better tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Erythromycin like an antibiotic? Am I getting an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. It is an antibiotic at higher doses, but we’re using it here for its motility effect, not because we think you have an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is up. I’m scared the nausea will come back full force.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable. The plan is to keep your nausea controlled with prochlorperazine as needed, keep your acid suppression going, and keep feeds at the rate you tolerate. We’ll only discharge once you’re stable on the regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now at Jevity 1.5 at 45 mL per hour, which is our goal rate. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, better than I expected. Still baseline nausea, but I’m not retching. Pain is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to keep monitoring your blood sugars and blood pressure as we step down the IV dextrose. If those stay stable, we’ll be close to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to keep trying to eat by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, focus on hydration and what you can tolerate. The main nutrition will be through the tube feeds. We don’t want you forcing solids if it triggers pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have remained stable on the goal tube feeds, and you’ve been hemodynamically stable. That’s what we needed to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow morning to make sure everything is set—supplies, teaching, and your medication list. I also want you comfortable with the feeding schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the feeding schedule again? I get confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. The plan is Jevity 1.5 at 45 mL per hour continuously, plus 200 mL bolus every 6 hours as prescribed. Nursing will also review how to flush the tube and what to do if there’s clogging or leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call you or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you can’t keep down fluids or meds, if you’re vomiting repeatedly, if you see blood or black material in vomit or stool, if you have fever or shaking chills, worsening abdominal pain, chest pressure, shortness of breath, or signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning—today is discharge day. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but okay. The feeds are running fine. I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly where we want you. Your discharge diagnosis is oral intake intolerance, and we’ve gotten you to goal tube feeds with manageable nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still being treated for an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your ulcer and reflux protection medications—pantoprazole and sucralfate—because of your history and symptoms. And we’re avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin because they can worsen ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What nausea meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have prochlorperazine as needed for nausea. Use it when nausea is limiting feeds or hydration, and be cautious about drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the erythromycin—how long do I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take erythromycin 250 mg every 6 hours as prescribed to help with motility. We’ll reassess at your follow-up visit based on how you’re tolerating feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already for depression and anxiety. Nothing here will mess with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home psychiatric medications—fluoxetine and aripiprazole—and your as-needed lorazepam. If you notice worsening mood, severe restlessness, or anything concerning, contact your outpatient prescriber as well as us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When do I see Dr. ___ again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in clinic as scheduled. The appointment details are in your discharge paperwork. Bring your tube-feeding log—rates, nausea episodes, and any low blood sugar symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, and tolerating goal tube feeds. If anything changes—vomiting, dehydration, bleeding, fever, worsening pain—please call or come back. We’ll see you soon in clinic.
